assignments.title: The morning brief
assignments.speaker: sal
assignments.brief: Aster’s update is in. Tell me what actually changed.

rows.detail: Profit is what remains after the costs shown.
Same company. Same currency. Compare the two periods.

rows.label: Draft headline
rows.detail: A headline is a claim. Check it against the figures.

evidence.prompt: Pin the two periods you need to check profit.

decision.prompt: What was Aster’s 2025 profit?

parts.text: Sales rose from $1,000 to $1,500.
Profit fell from $400 to $200.
Higher sales prove profit increased.

assignments.feedback: Sales rose. Profit fell. You found the part the headline missed. Your brief is on my desk.

assignments.title: Two companies, one call
assignments.speaker: shark
assignments.brief: Aster costs $5 a share. Helio costs $100. Which whole business has the smaller market value?

rows.label: Aster
rows.detail: Price multiplied by shares outstanding gives equity market value.

rows.label: Helio
rows.detail: Use the same calculation for both companies.

rows.label: Shark’s message
rows.detail: Price per share is not the value of the whole business.

evidence.prompt: Pin both companies for a fair comparison.

decision.prompt: Which has the smaller equity market value?

choices.label: Aster
choices.feedback: Count all the shares, not just the price of one.

choices.label: Helio
choices.feedback: Exactly: $100 × 100,000 = $10 million.

choices.label: They are equal
choices.feedback: Their share counts are different.

parts.text: Helio’s equity market value is $10 million.
Aster’s is $50 million; share price alone cannot establish value.
Aster must be cheaper because one share costs less.

assignments.feedback: You compared whole businesses. That is a useful comparison—not a buy recommendation.

assignments.title: Before the trade
assignments.speaker: oracle
assignments.brief: You have a possible idea. Decide how much room it deserves before pressing Buy.

rows.label: Desk cash
rows.detail: This is an authored planning example, not your live balance.

rows.label: Loss budget
rows.detail: This is the largest planned loss for this one idea.

rows.label: Review distance
rows.detail: For this exercise, calculate 5% of the position. Gaps could make a real loss larger.

evidence.prompt: Pin the loss budget and review distance.

decision.prompt: What position size gives a planned 5% loss of $20?
decision.hint: $20 divided by 0.05 is the position size. This is a plan, not a guarantee.

parts.text: A $400 position has a planned $20 loss at a 5% move.
A gap or execution delay could make the actual loss larger.
A review price guarantees a $20 maximum loss.

assignments.feedback: The size follows the plan. Keep the uncertainty in the note too.

assignments.title: A teammate needs a hand
assignments.speaker: wolf
assignments.brief: I’ve got the sales numbers. Can you send Sal an update?

rows.label: Sales
rows.detail: These figures compare last year with this year.

rows.label: Costs
rows.detail: You cannot calculate profit without costs.

rows.label: Wolf’s draft
rows.detail: This goes beyond the information supplied.

evidence.prompt: Pin the evidence and the missing information.

decision.prompt: How do you move this forward?
decision.hint: You can request the missing costs or send a carefully limited sales-only update.

choices.label: Ask Wolf for the costs
choices.feedback: Wolf is getting the missing cost report for you.

choices.label: Send a sales-only update
choices.feedback: Your update clearly says profit is still unknown.

choices.label: Send Wolf’s draft
choices.feedback: The draft makes a profit claim the figures cannot support.

parts.text: Sales increased from $1,800 to $2,400.
Profit cannot be assessed from this update alone.
Profit must have risen with sales.

assignments.feedback: Good. You kept the claim inside what the evidence can support. Wolf will follow up.

assignments.title: The follow-up
assignments.speaker: sal
assignments.brief: The costs are here. Revisit the update you prepared with Wolf.

rows.label: Earlier period
rows.detail: Earlier profit was $500.

rows.label: Latest period
rows.detail: Latest profit is sales minus costs.

rows.label: Source
rows.detail: This is the information missing from the earlier update.

evidence.prompt: Pin the two comparable periods.

decision.prompt: What changes in your update?

choices.label: Add the profit decline
choices.feedback: Your revised brief now includes the missing costs.

choices.label: Keep the earlier claim
choices.feedback: New evidence should change an unsupported claim.

choices.label: Say profit doubled
choices.feedback: The new figures show the opposite.

parts.text: Sales rose while profit fell from $500 to $200.
The new cost evidence changes the assessment.
The old profit claim still holds.

assignments.feedback: You returned to the evidence and updated your view. That is the job. First week filed.

responses.ask: You asked Wolf for costs. He has sent the report.
responses.qualify: You filed a sales-only update. Wolf has now sent the missing costs.

assignments.title: The small print adds up
assignments.speaker: shark
assignments.brief: This trade made a dollar before fees. Check what the desk actually kept.

rows.label: Purchase
rows.detail: The shares cost $100 before fees.

rows.label: Sale
rows.detail: The shares sold for $101 before fees.

rows.label: Fees
rows.detail: Include both sides when calculating the result.

evidence.prompt: Pin the sale and total fee evidence.

decision.prompt: What is the net result after both fees?

parts.text: The trade gained $1 before fees.
After $2 in fees, the result was a $1 loss.
A green price move always means a net gain.

assignments.feedback: You reconciled the receipt. Small fees can change the result of a small move.

assignments.title: More shares, same slice
assignments.speaker: sal
assignments.brief: A split changed the share count. Did it change your ownership?

rows.label: Before
rows.detail: The company had 100 shares total.

rows.label: After
rows.detail: The company now has 1,000 shares total.

rows.label: Desk chat
rows.detail: The count changed. Check the fraction and total value.

evidence.prompt: Pin the before and after records.

decision.prompt: What happened to your ownership fraction?

choices.label: Ten times larger
choices.feedback: The company’s total share count increased too.

choices.label: It stayed the same
choices.feedback: Both fractions are 1%.

choices.label: Ten times smaller
choices.feedback: Your share count also rose tenfold.

parts.text: The holding remains worth $100 in this example.
Ownership stays at 1% immediately after the split.
The split alone made the holding ten times more valuable.

assignments.feedback: Different number of slices. Same slice of the business.

assignments.title: A thin market
assignments.speaker: oracle
assignments.brief: The screen price looks good. The quote tells a different story.

rows.label: Small order
rows.detail: Estimated average price: about $2.02 per token.

rows.label: Large order
rows.detail: Estimated average price: about $2.22 per token.

rows.label: Last traded price
rows.detail: A last trade does not promise the price for your size.

evidence.prompt: Pin both order-size quotes.

decision.prompt: What is a defensible next step?
decision.hint: The larger order moves through worse prices. You can reduce size or wait.

choices.label: Investigate a smaller order
choices.feedback: A smaller size may reduce price impact; check a fresh quote.

choices.label: Wait for better liquidity
choices.feedback: Waiting is a valid decision; no order was placed.

choices.label: Assume $2 for all of it
choices.feedback: The size-specific quote contradicts that assumption.

parts.text: The larger order has a worse average quoted price.
A displayed last price is not a guaranteed fill.
Every order will fill at the last traded price.

assignments.feedback: You checked the price for the size you wanted. That matters more than a green number.

assignments.title: Yesterday’s headline
assignments.speaker: wolf
assignments.brief: This post is everywhere. Before I share it, check whether it is new.
assignments.sourceTitle: An update moving through the chat

rows.label: Repost date
rows.detail: The post appeared today.

rows.label: Original report
rows.detail: The figures describe the prior reporting period.

rows.label: Caption
rows.detail: A new repost does not make the underlying evidence new.

evidence.prompt: Pin the repost date and original report date.

decision.prompt: How should the update be described?
decision.hint: Use the original source date, not the date of a repost.

choices.label: Fresh company news
choices.feedback: The source itself is older.

choices.label: An older report being shared again
choices.feedback: That keeps the two dates clear.

choices.label: Definitely fabricated
choices.feedback: Age alone does not prove fabrication.

parts.text: The post is new, but the report is from April.
Check for a newer report before treating it as a fresh update.
A September repost makes April’s figures current.

assignments.feedback: Source checked. You stopped old information from dressing up as a new event.

assignments.title: Look at the whole desk
assignments.speaker: oracle
assignments.brief: One good run changed the shape of this portfolio. Show me where its risk sits.

rows.label: Aster
rows.detail: One issuer dominates this example.

rows.label: Helio
rows.detail: A second company.

rows.label: Cash
rows.detail: Cash is included in the total.

evidence.prompt: Pin the largest position and the cash reserve.

decision.prompt: What percentage of the desk is in Aster?

parts.text: Aster represents 70% of the portfolio.
A move in Aster could dominate the desk’s result.
Three lines on a portfolio mean equal diversification.

assignments.feedback: You found the concentration. Now it can be discussed rather than hidden in a total.

assignments.title: What do you actually own?
assignments.speaker: sal
assignments.brief: Two products use the same company logo. Compare the terms before treating them alike.

rows.label: Token A
rows.detail: Redemption is subject to issuer eligibility.

rows.label: Token B
rows.detail: Different legal structure and terms.

rows.label: Same logo
rows.detail: Company identity does not prove identical holder rights.

evidence.prompt: Pin both issuer term cards.

decision.prompt: What can you conclude?
decision.hint: The issuer terms—not the logo—describe the holder’s rights.

choices.label: They must grant the same rights
choices.feedback: The supplied term cards differ.

choices.label: The exposure is related; the rights differ
choices.feedback: Keep the issuer and terms attached to the instrument.

choices.label: Both grant voting rights
choices.feedback: Token A explicitly says it does not.

parts.text: Both products reference the same company.
Their rights and redemption terms differ.
A matching logo guarantees ordinary shareholder rights.

assignments.feedback: You separated the company from the instrument used to get exposure.

assignments.title: The right address
assignments.speaker: shark
assignments.brief: A convincing logo came with a new address. Check the identity before the desk uses it.

rows.label: Issuer registry
rows.detail: Illustrative identifiers; these are not real on-chain addresses.

rows.label: Shared listing
rows.detail: Look closely: one character differs.

rows.label: Listing artwork
rows.detail: Artwork can be copied.

evidence.prompt: Pin the registry identifier and listing identifier.

decision.prompt: What should happen next?
decision.hint: The strings differ. A logo is not evidence of contract identity.

choices.label: Pause and verify the exact mint
choices.feedback: The mismatch needs resolution.

choices.label: Trust the logo
choices.feedback: The logo does not resolve the mismatch.

choices.label: Choose whichever has more followers
choices.feedback: Popularity does not verify this contract.

parts.text: The listing identifier does not match the registry.
Pause and verify the exact contract before using it.
A familiar image is enough to establish identity.

assignments.feedback: You caught the mismatch before it became an order.

assignments.title: Two sides of a quote
assignments.speaker: oracle
assignments.brief: A bid and an ask are not the same price. Work out the cost of crossing the spread.

rows.label: Best bid
rows.detail: The displayed price to sell immediately at this size.

rows.label: Best ask
rows.detail: The displayed price to buy immediately at this size.

rows.label: Midpoint
rows.detail: The midpoint is not necessarily an executable price.

evidence.prompt: Pin the bid and ask.

decision.prompt: What is the spread per share?

parts.text: The spread is $0.20 per share.
The midpoint alone does not tell you the execution price.
Buying and selling immediately both happen at $10.00.

assignments.feedback: You can now explain the gap before a trade starts.

assignments.title: A bigger share count
assignments.speaker: sal
assignments.brief: A company issued new shares. Recalculate the slice held by an existing owner.

rows.label: Your holding
rows.detail: Your own number of shares did not change.

rows.label: Old total
rows.detail: Your earlier ownership was 10%.

rows.label: New total
rows.detail: Assume all shares have equal ownership rights.

evidence.prompt: Pin the holding and new total.

decision.prompt: What is the new ownership percentage?

parts.text: Ownership changed from 10% to 8%.
The holding’s share count stayed at 10.
An unchanged share count guarantees unchanged ownership.

assignments.feedback: The denominator matters. You explained the change without inventing a price prediction.

assignments.title: Send the useful version
assignments.speaker: wolf
assignments.brief: I need the week’s checks in one short hand-off. Help me leave out the claims we cannot defend.

rows.label: Instrument
rows.detail: Same company does not imply identical token rights.

rows.label: Identity
rows.detail: A logo alone does not verify a mint.

rows.label: Unverified claim
rows.value: A famous company cannot lose value
rows.detail: No source supports a guaranteed outcome.

evidence.prompt: Pin the two supported checks.

decision.prompt: What belongs in the hand-off?
decision.hint: Use the checks backed by evidence; leave out the guarantee.

choices.label: Terms, identity and order-size quote
choices.feedback: Those are concrete checks.

choices.label: The guaranteed-return claim
choices.feedback: The evidence offers no guarantee.

choices.label: Only the company logos
choices.feedback: Pictures omit the important distinctions.

parts.text: Check the issuer’s terms and exact contract identity.
Use the quote for the actual order size.
Familiar companies guarantee a positive return.

assignments.feedback: Clear, short and useful. The next person can act on the checks you actually made.

assignments.title: Getting back to even
assignments.speaker: shark
assignments.brief: This position fell from $100 to $80. Is a 20% gain enough to recover?

rows.label: Starting value
rows.detail: Use this to understand the original loss.

rows.label: Current value
rows.detail: A recovery percentage uses the current value as its base.

rows.label: Amount to recover
rows.detail: Compare this with $80, not $100.

evidence.prompt: Pin the current value and recovery amount.

decision.prompt: What gain from $80 gets back to $100?

parts.text: A 20% decline requires a 25% gain to recover.
The percentage base changes after the loss.
A 20% gain always cancels a 20% decline.

assignments.feedback: You used the right base. Same dollar gap, different percentage.

assignments.title: Who did we ask?
assignments.speaker: sal
assignments.brief: The team says everyone loves Aster. Read the trial results and fix the claim.

rows.label: People asked
rows.detail: They were selected for a product trial.

rows.label: Positive replies
rows.detail: Two testers did not like the product.

rows.label: Other customers
rows.detail: The trial cannot speak for all customers.

evidence.prompt: Pin the group definition and positive count.

decision.prompt: Which wording fits the evidence?
decision.hint: Keep both the count and the group in the statement.

choices.label: Everyone loves it
choices.feedback: Other customers were not surveyed.

choices.label: 8 of 10 beta testers liked it
choices.feedback: That names the count and the group.

choices.label: All beta testers liked it
choices.feedback: Two of the ten did not.

parts.text: 8 of 10 invited beta testers liked the product.
The trial does not establish what all customers think.
Everyone likes the product.

assignments.feedback: A small result can still be useful when its limits travel with it.

assignments.title: Leave room to breathe
assignments.speaker: oracle
assignments.brief: This desk needs a cash reserve. Work out how much is available for the proposed idea.

rows.label: Available cash
rows.detail: There are no pending orders in this exercise.

rows.label: Required reserve
rows.detail: Keep this available after the order.

rows.label: Estimated fees
rows.detail: Fees also come out of cash.

evidence.prompt: Pin the required reserve and fee allowance.

decision.prompt: What is the largest purchase before fees that keeps the reserve?

parts.text: The maximum purchase is $890 before fees.
That leaves $300 after the $10 fee.
All $1,200 is available for the purchase.

assignments.feedback: The plan includes what happens after the button is pressed.

assignments.title: The plan meets new evidence
assignments.speaker: wolf
assignments.brief: Our old note assumed costs would stay flat. The new update challenges that. What do we do with the note?
assignments.sourceTitle: A plan and a later update

rows.label: Earlier plan
rows.value: Review if operating costs rise over 10%
rows.detail: The review trigger was written before this update.

rows.label: New costs
rows.detail: Costs rose by $100 from a $500 base.

rows.label: Price today
rows.detail: A short-term price move does not erase the plan’s trigger.

evidence.prompt: Pin the original trigger and the new cost figures.

decision.prompt: What does the plan call for?
decision.hint: Costs rose 20%, crossing the plan’s 10% review trigger.

choices.label: Review the case against the new costs
choices.feedback: A review is due; buying or selling is a separate decision.

choices.label: Ignore it because the price rose
choices.feedback: That replaces evidence with a short-term price move.

choices.label: Sell automatically without reading
choices.feedback: The plan calls for review, not an automatic sale.

parts.text: Costs rose 20%, so the review trigger was reached.
Reassess the case; a review does not prescribe an automatic trade.
A green price means the earlier trigger can be ignored.

assignments.feedback: You followed a rule you wrote before the noise. Now make a fresh judgment.

assignments.title: Your first desk review
assignments.speaker: sal
assignments.brief: Bring me a decision you can explain: the evidence, the limit, and what would change your mind.

rows.label: Evidence
rows.value: A dated source and checked figures
rows.detail: Separate what was observed from what was assumed.

rows.label: Risk
rows.value: A position size and review trigger
rows.detail: A plan describes uncertainty; it cannot remove it.

rows.label: Outcome
rows.detail: A single gain or loss does not prove a process is sound.

evidence.prompt: Pin the evidence and risk-plan requirements.

decision.prompt: What makes a useful decision record?
decision.hint: A useful record can be checked and revisited even when the outcome disappoints.

choices.label: Only the final profit number
choices.feedback: The result omits how the decision was made.

choices.label: Evidence, limits and a reason to revisit
choices.feedback: Someone else can understand and review that record.

choices.label: A promise that the idea will work
choices.feedback: No decision record can guarantee the market’s response.

parts.text: Keep the evidence, assumptions and review trigger together.
Judge the process as well as the outcome.
A profitable result proves every part of the decision was right.

assignments.feedback: That is a desk I can hand work to. Your first twenty assignments are filed, and your decisions have a record.
